scope: India's civil nuclear power map: DAE and its ministers, NPCIL/ASHVINI/BHAVINI/UCIL, AERB and its statutory status, the SHANTI Act 2025 (what passed, when, what it permits, what remains unnotified), the Nuclear Energy Mission and the Bharat Small Reactor RFP, foreign vendor projects (Kudankulam/Rosatom, Jaitapur/EDF, Kovvada/Westinghouse), the Kaiga 5&6 and Mahi Banswara EPC contests, domestic equipment order flows (L&T, BHEL, MTAR, Godrej), uranium supply (UCIL, Kazatomprom), and private entrants (Tata Power, Adani, Hindalco, Reliance, JSW, JSPL). Deliberately left out: BARC's strategic/weapons programme, NFC and heavy-water plants, Gorakhpur/Chutka project detail beyond status, Cameco/TVEL/Uzbek supply contracts (dates only in WNA), and any person without a public office.

entities.label: SHANTI Act 2025
entities.sub: Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India Act — replaces AEA 1962 and CLND 2010
d: Introduced LS 2025-12-15; passed LS 2025-12-17; passed RS 2025-12-18; assent 2025-12-20; no committee referral; INDIA bloc walkout after JPC/standing-committee demand refused [documented]
Licences may go to government companies, JVs and 'any other company, except a company incorporated outside India' (PRS); Forbes India: foreign-controlled companies barred from licences [documented]

Permits private building, owning, operating and decommissioning of plants; fuel fabrication incl. conversion, refining and enrichment of U-235 'up to such threshold value'; reprocessing, heavy water and spent-fuel management reserved to Central Government [documented]
Graded operator-liability caps in Second Schedule, ₹100 cr–₹3,000 cr by capacity (PRS), replacing the uniform ₹1,500 cr cap; total cap 300 million SDR retained (Tharoor via CSDR) [documented]
Operator's statutory right of recourse against suppliers (CLND s.17(b)) removed; recourse only if provided by contract or damage from a deliberate act (Forbes India, PRS) [documented]
Appeals: Atomic Energy Redressal Advisory Council, then Appellate Tribunal for Electricity [documented]
As of 2026-08-05 the Act had not been notified into force ('will come into effect once the SHANTI Act is notified') [documented]

narratives.claim: The SHANTI liability amendments were written for US and French vendors.
narratives.strongestCase: The Act removes exactly the s.17(b) statutory supplier recourse that GE, Westinghouse and EDF cited as a barrier since 2010 (GE Hitachi withdrew 2015; EDF sought 'international-standard' liability protection 2016); Budget 2025 announced the amendments 'for active partnership with the private sector'; Congress MPs said so in the House.
narratives.strongestCounter: Foreign-incorporated companies are barred from holding licences; the Act primarily enables Indian private owner-operators (Tata Power, Adani, Hindalco) and domestic suppliers (L&T, BHEL, MTAR) who carried the same recourse exposure; Russia's Rosatom already operated under intergovernmental cover; nine months after assent neither EDF nor Westinghouse has signed anything. The 2010 Act was itself accused of being written for US vendors — the charge is symmetric.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A Jaitapur or Kovvada contract signed within 12 months of notification citing the recourse change; or DAE consultation records with vendors on the Second Schedule.

symmetryCheck: Control: the Congress-led UPA era (2008–2014), about which this file holds no theory. Applying the same lens — 'who benefited from the law change, and did money move' — produces an equally alarming picture: the 2008 Indo-US deal survived a confidence vote (2008-07-22) amid cash-for-votes allegations (₹9 crore alleged by three BJP MPs; JPC exonerated Amar Singh and Ahmed Patel on 2008-12-15); the 2010 CLND Act was attacked as drafted for GE/Westinghouse to unlock US insurance, with government denying US pressure; and CAG Report 38 of 2017 found NPCIL 'extending undue benefits to overseas collaborating partner' Atomstroyexport under contracts administered 2001–2014 (₹463 cr liquidated damages unclaimed). Conclusion: the lens generates 'law-written-for-vendor' and 'PSU-soft-on-contractor' findings under both governments, so those patterns are structural to a state-monopoly nuclear sector negotiating with a handful of foreign vendors, not evidence of a particular government's capture. What is asymmetric and therefore informative: (a) the 2025 Act was passed in four sitting days without committee referral, whereas the 2010 Act went through a standing committee; (b) the 2025 change flips the 2010 supplier-recourse position that BJP itself had demanded in opposition; (c) the domestic-private ownership door is new. Those three are the facts worth arguing about.
